subject: dwarfRifleman
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: dwarf rifleman with braided beard and blunderbuss.
Style: Blizzard/Warcraft.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a Warcraft-style dwarf rifleman: stocky build, braided beard, tricorn helmet, blunderbuss with flared muzzle, bandolier and powder horn, standing on a snowy rocky base with a barrel nearby. I need to structure this carefully as a TypeScript module since I won't be able to test it directly.

I'm sketching the skeleton layout — hips, spine chain up through chest, neck, and head — figuring out approximate coordinates and joint hierarchy to get believable dwarf proportions (short legs, wide shoulders, big head) at roughly 1.35m total height.

Now I'm working out body part construction using primitives like capsules for limbs, and nailing down leg dimensions — boot height, thigh/shin lengths, hip-to-ankle positioning — so the dwarf's stubby, bent-leg stance reads correctly.

Setting up the leg chains with joint hierarchies, defining hip-to-ankle limb points and boot geometry attached at the ankle joint, then moving on to position the shoulders and arms for the rifleman pose.

For the gun-holding pose, I'm weighing whether to keep arms separated like a neutral rest pose versus having the character actively grip the blunderbuss, settling on a compromise where one arm holds the gun at an angle while keeping the overall stance relaxed.

Computing arm joint positions and IK targets...

That's closer to straight, good, with elbow hint pulled back. I'll give the left hand a clenched fist with a chunky box/sphere shape plus thumb and gauntlet cuff, skipping the mug or flask idea for simplicity, and build the barrel-chested dwarf torso using loft/sweep of scaled boxes and spheres rather than a lathe.

I'm defining a blob helper using scaled low-poly spheres for chest and belly placement, then layering armor pieces like a breastplate and large pauldrons on top.

I'm picking a dwarf rifleman palette with Ironforge blue, gold, leather brown, ruddy skin, and ginger beard tones, then planning the signature oversized beard with two long braids down to the belt plus a mustache.

Writing braid geometry...

Then I'll shape the head with a heavy brow, big nose, and small eyes tucked under bushy eyebrows, placing the head joint accordingly.

Still working out eyes and nose...

I'm placing eyes just below the helmet brim using angular offsets around the head, with blue irises, pupils, and highlights drawn via SVG decal, plus separate sloped 3D brow boxes in beard color above them. Now thinking through the helmet shape itself, aiming for an Ironforge rifleman look with a leather or steel cap.

Going with a steel dome helmet featuring a studded gold band, leather crest ridge, extruded ear flaps, and a tuft of ginger hair peeking out underneath, plus brass goggles pushed up on top for a rifleman touch — made from two lathed rings with faintly glowing glass, connected by a strap loop sweeping around the dome.

Checking that the x=0 points on the lathe axis are fine since they're never negative, and positioning the head sphere with its scale and center so the helmet brim sits just above the eyebrows without clipping into the head's width at that height.

Working out the body proportions with a short, Warcraft-style neck so the head sits nearly on the shoulders — tracking boot, leg, hip, belly, chest, shoulder, and head heights to build a roughly 1.4m dwarf. Now I'm setting up the key coordinate variables for the head center.

Now I'm sketching the facial features: placing a bulbous nose sphere, ruddy cheek spheres, and curling handlebar mustache tubes that flare outward and up from under the nose. I'm shaping the beard mass as a front-facing wedge to cover the lower face, using swept or extruded geometry rather than a simple sphere cluster.

Switching approach: beard as three stacked ellipsoids (jaw puff, mid, lower) plus braids, painted ginger with grain streaks, positioned hanging from the chin down over the chest, making sure they sit far enough forward in z to clear the belly and chest surfaces.

I'm computing where two braids hang from the chin sides down past the belt, checking their z-depth against the belly's curved profile at each y-level so they clear it and sit visibly in front.

Now I'm figuring out the braid geometry itself, planning a helper that walks points along a path and places tilted, scaled ellipsoid segments at each step to build the twisted strand look.

For attaching the braids, I'm deciding whether to give them their own joint chains for animation or just hang them off the head bone directly—simpler to attach to head for now, but noting chain joints could let them swing later.

Three-point spans give three names, matching the braid chain naturally with role "tail". Now I'm thinking through the jaw structure: building a separate chin piece attached to a jaw joint beneath the skull, with the main beard puff also attached there, keeping the mouth closed and hidden under the mustache while still rigging the jaw joint for potential motion.

Then I'm working through small details like ears -- tiny visible spheres near the helmet line rather than hidden under flaps -- and considering adding decorative wing or emblem ornaments to the helmet sides, drawing on dwarf-helmet motifs like crossed hammers or mountain emblems for the design.

Now I'm sketching an anvil-and-hammer emblem to use as a decal on the chest tabard, and designing the tabard itself as an extruded cloth panel in blue with gold trim hanging from the belt, with the emblem placed as a textured plane layered just in front of the cloth surface.

For positioning, I'm hanging the tabard from the belt down to around the thighs, adjusting its front offset so it clears the belly curve at the top but still sits naturally against the legs lower down, and considering a slight tilt via rotation so it drapes more realistically rather than sitting perfectly flat.

For the pauldrons, I'm planning layered shoulder armor using scaled sphere domes positioned at each shoulder joint.

Now I'm adding a gold rim torus, studs, and a lower plate, tilted outward for the left and right sides, plus a gold collar/gorget at the neck and a leather bandolier with pouches and a powder horn across the chest.

I'm plotting the bandolier's drape path across the torso surface, defining a curved sequence of points from shoulder to hip that follows the chest and belly contours.

I'll give the bandolier a flat box cross-section rather than a round sweep so it reads as leather, and paint it accordingly. For the cartridge pouches, I'll skip aligning cylinders along the path tangent since that would make them lie flat against the strap, and instead attach small boxes where orientation doesn't matter as much.

Studs sticking outward along the surface normal feel like overkill, so I'll settle on simple pouches sized as thin boxes with brass flap details on top. For the belt, I'm planning a closed loop around the belly using a surface loop function, then sweeping a profile along that path.

For the buckle, I want a gold plate with an emblem positioned by casting a ray into the belly surface to find where it should attach, adjusting the loop height to y=0.62 so it reliably intersects the belly geometry rather than missing it.

Still weighing the belt approach between a loop and a torus shape—I'll stick with the surface-fitting loop method since it's the more tested path, accepting the exception risk for both belt and draped strap.

Beyond the belt, I'm planning the rifleman's gear: a backpack with bedroll, hanging tin cup, and small powder keg mounted on the chest bone, plus a detailed blunderbuss with wooden stock, flared brass barrel, iron bands, flintlock mechanism, trigger guard, and engraving.

Now I'm working through the positioning math for the gun in the hand—defining the grip point, barrel direction, and stock length, then checking whether the butt of the stock clips into the body or pauldron geometry given the chest width and arm position, concluding it passes just under the arm without overlap.

Simpler approach: keep the stock short since it's a blunderbuss, with grip-to-butt at 0.2 and grip-to-muzzle at 0.6. I'll start building the gun as a Group...

Defining gun part geometry...

Still shaping the barrel profile...

Writing the shading logic...

For colors I'm splitting the cannon into a blued-steel barrel with gold bands and a brass bell muzzle, built as two separate lathe profiles joined at the barrel-bell transition. I'm adding torus-ring bands along the barrel and starting to lay out a flintlock mechanism on the side with a lock plate, hammer, pan, and flint.

I'm now mirroring the lock plate onto both sides, adding a trigger guard loop and tiny trigger below the stock, and running a thin ramrod beneath the forestock. I'm also considering adding a small glowing ember sphere at the pan using a glow kit import for a subtle spark effect.

For materials, I'll build a custom `lit(base)` paint helper that shades by surface normal for a warm-top/cool-bottom stylized look, and pull in metal presets like brass, gilt, steel, and blued from a clockwork kit for the gun's hardware, keeping flat colors to a minimum since paints don't count against the palette limit. For the hands, I'm shaping a palm box with four finger bumps to suggest a gripping fist.

Now I'm designing the base: a rocky mountain plinth evoking an Ironforge-style pass, with a carved rune ring, snow patches, a powder barrel, and maybe a bullseye target tucked behind to nod at the Rifleman theme, while keeping the model centered and making sure the base stays below y=0 so the figure's feet properly contact the floor with only a tiny allowable sink.

Shifting the root could cause issues if other base parts are attached to it, so instead I could make the base thin enough—around 0.025, under the 2% tolerance of 0.029—letting it sink slightly below the floor with its top at y=0.

Rocks and snow mounds can rise above that slab to give it visual thickness without actually sinking too deep, with the boots resting at y=0 and sinking slightly into the snow surface. I'm thinking of making the slab a chunky octagonal cylinder with an added raised rim of stones around the perimeter to make the edge look thicker.

I'll add scattered props like a target stand, powder keg, and ammo crate at the back of the platform, plus a glowing rune ring decal laid flat on the ground near y=0.003 to avoid z-fighting with the top surface.

Now I'm sketching out the texture list: an eye texture, an anvil emblem for the tabard and gear, the glowing rune ring, a bullseye target design, and considering small decorative elements like a beard-tuft card or fur trim strip.

I'm continuing to plan textures — a hair-tuft card for beard wisps and fur accents, a full tabard panel texture with cloth trim and chevron border, a powder keg label with skull text, a bedroll stripe pattern for the backpack patch, and a goggle lens material.

For the beard, I'm sketching how to scatter hair cards: tapered blade shapes with root-to-tip gradients, scattered across the beard surface with minimum spacing, small card sizes, and a downward flow direction so they hang naturally along the jaw.

Now I'm moving to the skeleton rig, defining the joint hierarchy -- hips as root, then a spine chain through chest, neck, and head, each with position and aim targets to build the basic pose structure.

Then I'm adding a jaw joint under the head, and setting up leg chains from hip to knee to ankle, with named tip joints and a toe joint planned under the ankle for foot articulation.

For arms, I'm using a similar chain naming scheme with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints parented to the chest, positioning the shoulder points symmetrically off-center and tagging sides with L/R based on x-coordinate.

For hands, I'm considering whether to add finger digits to meet the rest pose requirement that limbs and digits appear separated and extended, though I want to keep the joint count manageable within the 160 limit by simplifying to a few finger chains per hand rather than fully articulated fingers.

I need to figure out finger placement using each hand's local coordinate frame, since the arms point in different directions (right forearm forward, left forearm down). I'll define finger bases at the palm edge and curl them inward toward the palm, though mapping "toward palm" in model space is getting complicated.

I'm reconsidering the grip geometry entirely—a gun's axis parallel to the forearm doesn't match how a fist actually wraps around a grip, which needs to be angled differently like a pistol grip. Maybe simplifying the hand to a chunky fist shape is the better path forward rather than fighting with precise forearm-to-stock alignment.

Still placing finger arcs around the grip...

I want fingers visible on the outer side since the inner side is hidden against the body, so I'll rotate about +f by roughly 260° starting from the top to wrap them around the forestock, using a grip radius near 0.036 and finger radius of 0.011. The thumb lies along the top-inner side pointing forward with two joints, and given the gun is being held, this wrapped-finger pose is a reasonable compromise against the strict "fingers extended and separated" rest pose.

For the left hand I'm going relaxed instead: fingers slightly curled and splayed, hanging naturally with the palm facing inward toward the thigh, curling toward that inward direction. I'm spacing the fingers front-to-back along z with index forward and pinky back, and positioning each knuckle out along the forearm direction from the wrist.

Still writing finger curves...

For the palm itself I'll use a simple oriented box aligned to the forearm direction, and I'll wrap this all into a helper function for building hands, with a similar approach planned for the gauntlet.

Adding color bands to transition sleeve into bracer at the elbow, then setting up the same sweep approach for legs.

Still working out foot box dimensions...

Now placing hip root and shoulder joints, with the right arm bent to hold the gun target, elbow hinting outward and back. The pauldron attaches at the shoulder joint offset up and outward so it follows rotation naturally, and now I'm starting the paint helper for the tunic's blue coloring.

I need to double-check which SDK functions are actually exported from the builder package before importing them, since some names like vec or DEG might live elsewhere.

Writing shading helper function...

I'm confirming the rng helper signature and planning the part-building API shape with scale, bone, and texture options, then sketching a sphere helper function for constructing body geometry.

For painted surfaces, I'm estimating texel density based on total painted area versus the paint atlas resolution, considering whether 2048 gives enough detail across the roughly 8 square meters being painted.

I'll stick with the default 1024 atlas since the painted areas aren't too large, and now I'm starting to set up the imports and builder code.

Writing import statements...

Now I'm defining the color palette constants—blues, golds, leather tones, skin, beard colors, wood, steel, snow, stone—and sketching out the paint definitions like a tonal blue with cloth weave noise and a gilt metal finish for gold trim.

Defining rock material with mottled coloring, then adding a conditional paint rule so upward-facing surfaces get snow-capped while other faces stay rocky.

For wood, I'm setting up a grain texture with brown tones. Then for the eye, I'm sketching an SVG with an almond-shaped eye socket, dark outline, blue iris, and pupil highlight.

Writing eye SVG...

I need to clip the iris to the eye shape and account for stroke width scaling at raster size. For attaching the eye as a decal onto the head sphere, I'm figuring out the right parameters for positioning it on the surface using the hit point and normal.

Now I'm sketching out the emblem SVG design: a dark blue shield circle with a gold ring border, and a gold anvil shape built from a path with tapered horn and base details.

For the tabard, I'm designing it as a single textured plane shaped like a pennant with a V-shaped bottom cutout, blue field with gold border, and the anvil emblem embedded directly inside it rather than using a separate extruded mesh—keeping it flat since the cloth doesn't need thickness.

Now I'm working out the geometry for tilting the plane to match the body's curvature: rotating it slightly around the X-axis so the bottom edge recedes backward while the top stays forward, then solving for the correct center position in Y and Z so the top aligns with the belt line and the surface follows the belly and thigh curve naturally.

For the ground decoration, I'm planning an SVG rune ring: a transparent canvas with two concentric circles in light blue stroke, plus twelve glyph marks spaced evenly around the ring using rotation transforms to position each small rune symbol.

Drawing the archery target now, concentric red/white rings with a gold bullseye and scattered bullet holes.

I also need to work out the target stand placement and orientation -- it should face toward +Z, the direction the dwarf is shooting, so I need to figure out where in front of the dwarf it can sit without blocking the main view.

I could place a powder keg with a label facing front, a crate with an emblem, and a pile of snow-covered rocks with a small signpost reading "IRONFORGE →" in the back-left.

Working out positions: signpost on the left side opposite the gun arm, keg and crate placed at specific back coordinates, with the rune ring sized smaller than the base radius so the props sit on the outer edge.

I'm now realizing the gun muzzle extends beyond the base radius when the arm points forward, so I'm adjusting by enlarging the base into an ellipse and angling the gun diagonally upward in a "port arms" ready stance, calculating where the muzzle and stock ends land to keep everything visually contained within the figure.

I'm working out the forearm-to-hand connection so the fingers wrap naturally around the grip, and setting up the lathe geometry for the gun's profile along its directional axis, with roll orientation not mattering for this shape.

For the lock plate, I decide to place it on the +X side facing the viewer with a wooden cheek piece opposite, plus a brass sideplate detail. I compute the gun's local up vector using a cross product between the forward direction and the side axis to get proper perpendicular orientation for the hardware placement.

Defining the gun's forward vector...

Now I'm placing a powder horn on the hip, curving it as a swept cone shape with a brass cap and strap, positioned near the left hip and attached to the hips bone with a cream-to-dark horn coloring.

I'm also adding a leather pouch on the right hip and a backpack on the chest: a leather box with a flap, a bedroll cylinder lashed on top with striped paint, and shoulder straps drawn as curved sweeps running from the pack over the shoulders down to the front chest.

Still working out how these straps drape over the chest's curved surface so they don't clip through it, adjusting the path points and considering a draping function that follows the body's geometry.

For the collar, I'm adding a gold gorget torus around the neck, which should be mostly hidden by the beard anyway -- and I'm deciding against a fur mantle since the rifleman reference doesn't call for one.

With hands and arms settled, I'm now thinking through tapered sweep radii for the arms, using keyed number arrays to shrink the limb from shoulder through elbow to wrist for a natural taper.

For the legs I'm planning similar tapered sweeps, thicker at the thigh and narrowing toward the ankle, with boot shafts as separate wide-cuff cylinders covering the shin so the proportions read correctly at the knee-to-ankle transition.

I'm riding the boot geometry on the knee joint bone so it bends naturally with the leg, then adding gold-trimmed steel knee guards as small blobs positioned just in front of the knee joint.

For the dwarf's outfit, I'm planning brown trousers with darker leather boots accented by gold buckles. For the belt, I'm sweeping a box-section loop around the waist, working through the uncertainty of how the cross-section should orient (sideways vs. vertical) and leaning toward a roughly square profile so it reads as a thick leather strap rather than a rope.

For the belt buckle, I'm raycasting to find the belly's front surface and placing a gold box there, figuring out the local axes so the box sits flush with proper width, thickness, and height, then planning a decal emblem on its face.

Skipping the shoulder emblem for now and putting the main emblem on the tabard instead. With the setup reasoned through, I'm ready to start writing the actual build function, aiming for roughly 250 parts using loops, starting with the builder initialization and skeleton structure.

Defining joint hierarchy for hips, spine, chest, neck, head, and jaw...

I'm thinking a full geometric vest piece is too complex, so instead I'll fake the leather vest look with position-based paint logic—coloring chest areas blue versus leather depending on x/z coordinates.

Writing paint function logic...

But I realize the beard will cover the central chest area, so the lacing detail would be hidden anyway. I should shift the decorative elements to vertical trim lines at the vest edges instead, keeping the leather vest visible outside that zone.

Rather than overcomplicate the chest, I'll rely on simple tonal painting for the tunic weave and add richness through pauldrons, a bandolier, belt, tabard, and backpack straps -- including a leather harness forming an "X" across the front from the shoulder straps.

Now moving to the head: I'm building the skull as a detailed blob for decal quality, adding a heavy brow ridge mostly hidden by the helmet, and shaping angled brow boxes with rotation to give an angry expression where the outer edges lift.

Working out the brow rotation direction, then positioning hair cards and eye decals just below the brows at the appropriate elevation around the skull sphere.

Now I'm placing facial features: a bulbous nose with a cold-tinted reddish hue and tiny nostril bumps, rosy cheek blobs, and pointed ear blobs with a small gold earring torus on the left side.

Working out the jaw and mouth region — the lower jaw blob covers where the mouth would be, but since the mustache and beard will hide it entirely, I'm skipping teeth and lip details and just adding a hint of a dark mouth slit underneath for depth. Now moving to sculpting the mustache as swept tube paths curving outward from the center along the cheek.

For the beard, I'm deciding attachment logic: the first beard piece parents to the jaw so it moves naturally with speech, but the lower beard masses attach to the head instead so they don't swing too wildly when the jaw opens, treating the braids as a chained parent structure off the head.

Working through B1's placement covering cheeks and jaw beneath the mustache, then checking B2's position against the chest surface so it sits slightly in front rather than clipping, and verifying B3 against the belly curvature to keep it floating just outside the torso surface.

For B4, the tapering tip, I'm making sure it ends near the belt without excessive embedding into the belly. Now I'm mapping out the hanging braids as paths extending from the beard's lower corners outward and down, checking each waypoint against the chest's surface curve to keep them clear of the torso.

For the braid structure itself, I'm defining link spheres that taper in radius along the length, nine links total, finishing with a gold ring and tassel at the end, deciding to use the beard's grain paint for texture and slight rotation offsets on alternating links for a twisted look. I'm also confirming that the path's `.at(t)` method returns a position vector so I can place each link correctly along the curve.

Now I'm wiring the braid into the chain system, attaching it near the head joint with a Catmull-Rom path through four control points, which gives three segments and matching joint names. For the helmet, I'm setting up a lathed dome shape positioned just above and slightly forward of the head, defining its cross-sectional profile from base to peak to get a rounded, tapering silhouette.

I'm picking a dark steel paint with slight tarnish for a cool Ironforge feel, then checking clearances—the dome's base radius risks overlapping the brow geometry at the helmet's rim, so I'm nudging the helmet's vertical position up slightly to clear the brows while keeping the overall height within target, leaving a small visible gap of forehead between the brow line and the helmet's base.

Now I'm verifying the dome fully encloses the skull's crown with margin to spare, and sketching out a decorative gold rim band with a ring of ten stud spheres seated around its base using a ring-placement helper that orients each stud outward along the band.

Since literal frame placements won't carry a bone reference automatically, I decide to explicitly pass the head bone to the stick options for the studs to be safe. Then I move on to designing a crest ridge running front-to-back over the dome, planning an extruded arch outline that conforms to the dome's curvature.

Still defining the ridge outline...

Making the crest gold instead of blue, with smoothing off for crisp edges, positioned so it intersects the dome slightly but stays geometrically valid with no self-intersections. Now moving on to the cheek flaps.

For these, I'm defining a hanging side plate shape extruded along the X axis, positioned near the side of the head slightly outside the dome surface so it floats a bit like a steel flap, with the bottom edge angled inward to follow the jawline.

I'll skip the gold wings idea and instead add a small brass finial cone at the top of the crest. I'm considering a plume or feather texture but will leave that out for simplicity.

Now I'm positioning goggles pushed up onto the helmet's front brim, using two angled lens cylinders aimed along the dome's forward-up slope, and calculating their placement based on the dome's curvature and normal direction around height 1.34-1.37.

I'm also adding a leather strap as a torus wrapped horizontally around the helmet at y≈1.31, sized to hug the dome's radius at that height.

Now I'm giving the goggle lenses a glowing teal tint, then adding ginger hair details: sideburn tufts under the helmet sides, a merged beard, and a small clump of back hair for texture.

Writing eyebrow and fur scatter logic...

I'm also adding a hanging tin cup and coiled rope at the hip for extra character detail, plus working out pauldron domes on each shoulder bone with scaled spheres and slope rotation for armor plating.

Still writing pauldron geometry...

I'm deciding against adding a fur trim or emblem to the pauldron, keeping the design simpler with just a dome shape instead.

I'm working out the exact placement math for the dome pauldron relative to the shoulder and head, checking that its radius and offset keep it clear of the head sphere and properly nested against the chest and arm geometry.

For the base prop, I'm sketching a flat octagonal cylinder scaled elliptically in z to form the stone base, deciding to attach it to the hips bone since props don't need their own rig, though I'm weighing whether that risks unwanted movement if hips get animated later.

I'm resolving the hierarchy issue by introducing a single "root" joint at the origin with hips as its child, so the base can stay bone-rooted while hips stays free to animate. Now I'm planning the snow drift detail on the base rim, placing a ring of flattened rock and snow blobs using deterministic random angles and elliptical radius positions around the rim.

For the top surface I'm designing a paint function that blends a cobblestone texture in the center with snow coverage near the edges, using an elliptical radius check against the normal direction to decide which pattern applies at each point.

Now I'm adding a glowing rune-covered plane facing upward near the base, sized to sit just above the surface with the right orientation so the rune texture reads correctly from above.

I'm positioning rock clusters symmetrically around the octagonal base rim, then starting to place prop objects like a small keg cylinder near the edge.

For the keg, I'm shaping it with a lathe profile to get a bulging wooden barrel silhouette, adding iron hoop torus bands near top and bottom, and planning a decal label on the curved front surface using a ray cast to find the correct placement point.

Now I'm adding a wooden crate nearby with a slight rotation, thinking about metal corner strips and a snow cap on top, plus starting on a signpost built from a thin cylinder post.

Still designing the arrow plank with a transparent texture overlay for the "IRONFORGE" text...

I'm checking for object overlaps near the dwarf's left hand and signpost, then repositioning the keg and crate to avoid collisions in the back-left area of the scene.

With the layout settled at roughly 300 parts, I'm planning the code structure carefully, making sure to only import the specific utility functions I actually need (builder, curves, color helpers, noise/texture functions, SVG rendering) to avoid unused-import errors under strict typechecking.

Writing imports and shading logic...

Mixing in the mud color for the lower portion, then settling on a small flat color palette—dark browns, white for texture, cyan for lens highlights, orange for sparks and flame—since paints don't need to be extensive here.

Defining a helper function to create blob-shaped sphere parts with configurable color, position, bone attachment, and scale, keeping types loose with generic object options to avoid fighting TypeScript's strictness.

I'm also typing the point-like position parameter as either a coordinate array or a Vector3, allowing flexible color input types for parts, and sketching a cylinder-aiming helper that connects two points with a tapered radius and bone attachment for rod-like shapes.

For the rod sides, I'm defaulting to flat-faceted shading at 8 sides rather than smooth shading by passing a smooth:false option. Now I'm working out the limb helper signature taking root, target, segment lengths, and bend directions, and I'm checking the hip-to-ankle leg geometry to make sure the knee bends forward correctly given the joint positions.

I'm figuring out the arm chains next, computing shoulder-to-wrist distances to decide how straight or bent each elbow should be, then setting bend direction vectors for left and right arms accordingly. Now I'm writing the hand joint logic, referencing the wrist and elbow joints from the arm chain to orient the hand pose.

Working out palm box dimensions and orientation...

Now mapping out finger chains: four base points offset across the palm, with curl points bending inward toward the body for each knuckle segment.

Thumb chains run from the palm side at an angle, with distinct chain names for each digit and joint, and I'll use tapered sweep radii with rounded caps to give the glove fingers a tapered, fleshy shape.

For the right hand grip, I'm setting up the palm as a block positioned relative to the wrist and forearm, then defining finger arcs as circular paths around an axis—computing each finger's center point, start position, and sweep angle so the fingers curl naturally around the grip, with four parallel offsets spacing the fingers along the gun's axis and each finger built as a three-joint chain.

Now I'm working out the thumb's starting position on the inner side of the palm, plus adding knuckle bumps as small spheres where each finger path begins.

I'm positioning the forearm approaching the wrist from above/behind, and adding a gauntlet cuff cylinder near the wrist for the gun arm's gloved look.

Now I'm building the stock geometry — boxes for the stock body, butt, buttplate, and comb, attached to the wrist bone with wood and brass materials.

Still blocking out the gun parts...

I'm checking that the bell polygon points don't self-intersect, verifying the inner wall stays within the outer contour at each height, and deciding to keep sharp edges with no smoothing for now.

Now I'm working out the gun's finer details—placing gold decorative bands as tori along the barrel axis with varying radii, adding a brass tang strip along the comb, and positioning the steel lock plate on the side before moving on to the hammer.

I'm building out the lock mechanism pieces: the hammer and its hook shape using angled boxes, the brass flint jaw, the pan, the frizzen, and finally a small glowing sphere to represent a spark at the firing point.

Now I'm working out the trigger guard as a half-torus, figuring out how to orient and rotate it so the curve bows downward correctly, reasoning through the axis and "up" parameters to get the bulge direction right.

The gun's overall silhouette with its flared brass muzzle looks solid, so I'm moving on to designing the powder horn's curved sweep path using a bezier/catmull-rom spline.

Writing sweep path and shading...

Now I'm adding the brass cap at the horn's wide end, a leather pouch with gold button on the right rear hip, and positioning a backpack on the chest bone with box dimensions set against the back curve.

Adding the pack flap with a rear-facing emblem for visibility from behind, plus a horizontal cylinder bedroll strapped to the chest bone near the pack.

Skipping pickaxe and pick ideas for now. I'm defining the torso surface from chest and belly profile points, then sketching a rough bandolier path across the chest and down the side.

For the strap's cross-section, I'm working out which radius should face outward versus which should hug the surface, settling on a small asymmetric width-by-thickness pair to give it a flat, ribbon-like shape as it wraps diagonally across the chest.

For the belt, I'm reasoning through the path orientation going counterclockwise around the vertical axis, tracking how the tangent and normal vectors rotate so the cross-section stays properly aligned as it loops horizontally.

I'm setting up the shoulder straps and bandolier geometry, then placing cartridge pouches along the draped path by sampling points at even intervals and snapping them to the torso surface, with each pouch modeled as a small box with a brass cylindrical cap on top.

I'll skip adding a dagger sheath and a neck gorget to keep the rifleman's kit simpler.

For glow details, I'll add small glowing frost rune gems embedded in the center of each pauldron dome, generating a rune glyph function to draw those SVG markings.

Writing SVG glyphs...

Adjusting stroke widths and glyph scaling...

I'm now designing the keg label texture with a parchment background, bold "POWDER" text, and a bomb icon, plus a separate sign texture with "IRONFORGE" lettering in gold with a dark outline.

For the crate, I'm adding wood grain planks with iron corner strips, and creating a circular emblem with a blue shield, gold trim, and a crossed-axe design rotated at an angle.

Writing anvil path code...

Now I'm designing the tabard shape with a diamond-pointed bottom, a gold inner border, and a scaled-down emblem embedded near the top, plus small fringe details at the hem. I'm finalizing the icon list: sign, label, eye, emblem, tabard, runes, tuft, and badge, having dropped the target icon.
